summary: This clipped Hinterland Who's Who fact sheet describes Canada's boreal forest, covering its size and location, plant and animal life, wetlands, and the benefits it provides. It also covers threats such as habitat loss, climate change and development, and outlines actions by governments, environmental groups, industry and individuals to protect it. Navigation menus and site boilerplate were ignored.
one_line: A Hinterland Who's Who fact sheet on the boreal forest's extent, species, ecological benefits, threats and conservation actions.
key_facts: The boreal forest makes up almost one third of the world's forests, stretching round the northern parts of North America and Eurasia.
Canada contains about a third of the northern forest, named after Boreas, the Greek god of the North Wind.
The boreal region stretches more than 5 000 km from Newfoundland and Labrador in the east to Yukon in the west, and occupies more than half of Canada's land area.
The boreal region contains more than 1.5 million lakes and is home to more than four million people, including most of Canada's Aboriginal people.
Wetlands occupy 30 percent of Canada's boreal forest and filter millions of litres of water every day.
Wetlands provide breeding, moulting, and staging habitat for more than 13 million ducks, about 40 percent of the North American duck population.
Nearly half of the birds in North America rely on the boreal forest at some time during the year.
The boreal forest shelters more than 85 species of mammals, and an estimated 32 000 insect species inhabit Canada's boreal forest.
Canada's boreal forest is home to about 130 species of fish.
The Canadian boreal forest is home to about two thirds of Canada's 140 000 species of plants, animals, and micro-organisms.
Forests hold between 20 and 100 times more carbon than do agricultural crops, and they keep the carbon for longer periods.
The most well-known species at risk in the boreal region include some populations of woodland caribou, the wood bison, the Peregrine Falcon, the Yellow Rail, and the Whooping Crane.
The snowshoe hare is the most ecologically important boreal mammal because it is a food source for many predators and feeds on many plants and shrubs.
The fact sheet was produced with support from FPAC and the Model Forest Network and is copyrighted by Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada, 2006.
